title: A major NFT marketplace is shutting down—5 years after the boom, there's a lesson for investors
description: Five years ago, NFTs seemed to be everywhere.Although the digital collectibles, known as nonfungible tokens, had existed since 2014, they exploded in
body: Five years ago, NFTs seemed to be everywhere.Although the digital collectibles, known as nonfungible tokens, had existed since 2014, they exploded in popularity in 2021 alongside the cryptocurrency boom, becoming status symbols for celebrities and wealthy collectors.Weekly NFT trading volume across major blockchains surged from about $4.4 million in late 2020 to a peak of $3.2 billion in August 2021, according to CryptoSlam data published by The Block.Today, much of that trading activity has disappeared. Weekly NFT trading volume has fallen more than 99% since August 2021, and several major NFT marketplaces have closed. On Thursday, Blur, once the largest marketplace for Ethereum-based NFTs, shut down its website.At the height of the boom, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey sold an NFT of his first tweet for $2.9 million, while a digital artwork by an artist known as Beeple fetched $69.3 million at Christie's. Paris Hilton and Jimmy Fallon showed off their Bored Ape NFTs on "The Tonight Show," and even McDonald's released NFTs celebrating the return of its McRib sandwich.Back then, some buyers believed NFTs represented the future of digital ownership, while others bet they could resell them at higher prices. But as enthusiasm faded, so did the demand that had driven the digital tokens' values higher.The NFT boom and bust shows how quickly speculative investments can unravel when demand dries up. For investors, it's a cautionary tale about spotting the warning signs before buying into the next craze, financial experts tell CNBC Make It.Why did NFTs collapse?Part of the initial appeal of NFTs was the promise of a new way for artists and other creators to make money from their work. Using blockchain technology, NFTs allowed creators to sell digital collectibles with verifiable ownership records and potentially earn royalties on subsequent sales through smart contracts.More broadly, NFTs were touted as part of the future of digital ownership, with the potential to transform how people bought, sold and traded digital assets.But establishing ownership of a digital collectible was different from creating lasting demand for it, says Evan Mills, a financial advisor at wealth management firm Scholar Advising. "NFTs tried to manufacture that demand," he says. "Blockchain could establish who owns the token, but it couldn't guarantee that anyone would really value the ownership at the end of the day."In practice, many of the NFTs that attracted attention were relatively simple digital images, such as cartoon animals or promotional artwork featuring beer cans.Traditional collectibles, such as paintings, antiques and baseball cards, have established histories and communities of collectors that can sustain demand, Mills says. NFTs, by comparison, became enormously popular in a relatively short period.Unlike many traditional collectibles, however, NFTs could be created in virtually unlimited quantities. While individual collections might contain a limited number of tokens, there was little stopping creators from launching new series. At the height of the boom in 2022, roughly 500 new NFT collections were being created every day, according to blockchain analytics firm IntoTheBlock.The rapid rise in NFT prices helped fuel expectations that buyers would continue paying more for them. But as enthusiasm faded, so did the pool of potential buyers.And unlike stocks or bonds, most NFTs didn't generate income, meaning buyers hoping to turn a profit generally depended on someone else being willing to pay more for them, says Martin Mulyadi, the YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting at Shenandoah University."Most NFTs paid nothing, so the only way to make money was finding a next buyer at a higher price," he says. "When the buyers stopped coming, there was nothing holding up the price." What everyday investors can learnFor everyday investors, the NFT bust is a reminder that an asset's popularity doesn't necessarily make it a worthwhile investment.One common justification for buying risky investments like collectibles is that they make up only a small portion of an otherwise diversified portfolio. Financial advisors often recommend limiting speculative holdings to money an investor can afford to lose. But keeping an investment small doesn't necessarily make it worthwhile, Mulyadi says."While keeping a bet small limits the damage, it doesn't turn a weak asset into a good one," he says.Mills argues that investors can also confuse speculation with diversification."Diversification is not just owning more things," he says. "It's owning things that have different economic characteristics that change the risk and return of your overall portfolio."For collectibles, that means looking beyond an item's scarcity or popularity to whether there's an established market of buyers likely to value it over time. Even then, future demand can be difficult to predict. There's also a difference between buying a collectible because you actually like it and buying it because you think someone else will pay more for it. For many NFT speculators, the appeal was likely less about owning what was essentially a JPEG than the prospect of reselling it for a profit.Before buying a speculative asset, Mills recommends asking two questions: What is the economic reason it should generate a return, and what role does it play in the overall portfolio? If an investor can't answer those questions, he says, the investment may not belong in the portfolio at all."A bad investment doesn't become a good investment just because you only own a little bit of it," Mills says.

schema.headline: A major NFT marketplace is shutting down—5 years after the boom, there's a lesson for investors

title: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
description: watch nowBillionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annu
body: watch nowBillionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annual charitable giving from the prior year.Buffett, 96, converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation — the foundations run by his three children, Susie, Howard and Peter Buffett.  Following the donations, the chairman emeritus of Berkshire still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion. "Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought," wrote Buffett, who was succeeded as chairman in September by his son Howard, in his annual Thanksgiving message. The letter was much shorter than his message last Thanksgiving. Charlie Munger, former vice chairman of Berkshire, passed away in November 2023.Berkshire shares have been on a tear recently, up more than 19% since the start of the fourth quarter and ending last week with four consecutive record high closes. That compares with the S&P 500's decline of 1.2% so far for the fourth quarter. Berkshire has been seen as a safe haven as investors have worried about the artificial intelligence buildout, corporate drama and geopolitical risk. The shares are now outperforming the S&P 500 for the year by about 7.5 percentage points. In his letter, Buffett reiterated that all of his Berkshire shares eventually will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal being to increase the size of the grants each year. Confidence in BerkshireBuffett wrote that the gifts were a signal of his confidence not only in his three children, but also in Berkshire CEO Greg Abel: "My children have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity. ... You heard plenty from me in September about my confidence in Berkshire. That confidence is as strong as ever," he said.Referring to Munger and himself, Buffett added, "Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received.""Warren continues to share his wisdom with us all during this holiday season. His example reflects the kindness he encourages in all of us," said CEO Abel of the letter.Buffett closes his message with this advice: "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."

schema.headline: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter

title: Prediction market odds for Tesla-SpaceX merger by April 2027 top 60%
description: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesOdds of a SpaceX and Tesla merger before March 2027 have climbed to 62% from 27% on Kalshi since Thursday.Chances tha
body: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesOdds of a SpaceX and Tesla merger before March 2027 have climbed to 62% from 27% on Kalshi since Thursday.Chances that Elon Musk's two companies, SpaceX, a satellite and rocket maker, and Tesla, an electric vehicle manufacturer, will soon integrate have jumped since late last week across multiple Kalshi markets. The contract asks, "When will Tesla and SpaceX merge?" and would be verified by news outlets and the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR database. On Friday, Walter Isaacson, a CNBC contributor and author of a Musk biography, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" he's confident a merger is coming. He cited Terafab, the semiconductor project involving Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, as a catalyst."I think you have to have a merger. Makes no sense otherwise," Isaacson said. Tesla's 2026 annual shareholder meeting, set for Dec. 3, may provide more insight into a potential linkup, Isaacson said. While speculators are anticipating an announcement of a merger this year, a research note from Jefferies last week said a deal will likely face backlash after the Democrats won control of Congress and several key governorships in the midterm elections earlier this month. "We understand there is higher risk of scrutiny post elections, but the vision of a combined SpaceX and Tesla as proxies for longer-term U.S. national strategies of independence and leadership in space, energy, manufacturing or semiconductors, in our view, remain highly relevant regardless of which party controls Congress," wrote Jefferies analyst Philippe Houchois. Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson, a Democrat, said a possible merger between Musk's two companies would face "tremendous scrutiny," Bloomberg reported Thursday. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Prediction market odds for Tesla-SpaceX merger by April 2027 top 60%

title: U.S. crude oil declines to $85 a barrel on recovering Middle East exports
description: Oil prices rose on Wednesday after falling to two-month lows in the previous session, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the Ira
body: Oil prices rose on Wednesday after falling to two-month lows in the previous session, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the Iran war and concerns about ongoing attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.Eli Hartman | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesOil prices are falling Monday as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz recover and tensions between Iran and the U.S remain at a stalemate.Brent crude fell 3.55% to $92.44 per barrel Monday while West Texas Intermediate crude futures settled down 3.58% to $85.39 a barrel.The International Energy Agency said on Friday it expects global supply to exceed 1.7 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter of 2026, reversing its earlier forecast for a deficit as Middle East exports recover faster than global demand and even as shipping attacks continue.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconWTI Crude, YTDMeanwhile, Russia's crude oil production rose to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, a 210,000 barrel-a-day surge, according to the IEA.Goldman Sachs said in a Sunday note it expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and fall to $78 by December 2027 as the market returns to a surplus. The bank believes Middle East supply to rise above its 2025 average as producers use ship-to-ship transfers and add pipeline capacity.

schema.headline: U.S. crude oil declines to $85 a barrel on recovering Middle East exports

title: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
description: [The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday h
body: [The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road.""I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy. In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint.""After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

schema.headline: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’

title: Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond
description: Actor Robert Pattinson at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Sept. 5th, 2026. Laurent Koffel | Gamma-rapho | Getty ImagesRobert Pattinson has been cast
body: Actor Robert Pattinson at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Sept. 5th, 2026. Laurent Koffel | Gamma-rapho | Getty ImagesRobert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise.Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."Pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic. The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."In 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios, which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion. Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond

title: United Airlines resolves system outage that affected departing flights
description: United Airlines passenger planes are seen at gates at Newark Liberty International Airport in Newark, New Jersey, Nov. 15, 2026.Charly Triballeau | Af
body: United Airlines passenger planes are seen at gates at Newark Liberty International Airport in Newark, New Jersey, Nov. 15, 2026.Charly Triballeau | Afp | Getty ImagesUnited Airlines on Monday said it had resolved a "widespread system outage" that briefly affected departing flights."We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures," the airline said in a statement. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.A United spokesperson said there was no indication that the outage was a cyberattack.The Air Line Pilots Association, which represents pilots for United and other carriers, said in an earlier message to members seen by CNBC that the operational outage was "affecting multiple pilot facing applications" and that United could not "provide outbound flights with final weights."United's outage came three days after a nationwide ground stop halted departures across the country for more than four hours, snarling travel and leading to widespread delays and cancellations over the weekend.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the issues that led to Friday's ground stop on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over from copper wires to fiber optic.There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data. There was no indication that United's outage Monday was related to the issues that caused Friday's ground stop.— CNBC's Leslie Josephs and Phil LeBeau contributed to this report.

schema.headline: United Airlines resolves system outage that affected departing flights

title: Berkshire Hathaway raised its stake in Delta in the third quarter. It also trimmed a key bank holding
description: President and CEO of Berkshire Hathaway Greg Abel attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort
body: President and CEO of Berkshire Hathaway Greg Abel attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 8, 2026. Brendan McDermid | ReutersBerkshire Hathaway made several moves in the stock market during the third quarter, adding to key positions and trimming others. The Omaha-based conglomerate, now led by CEO Greg Abel, increased its Delta Air Lines stake by 12%, scooping up 7.13 million shares. The position was worth $5.37 billion at the end of the third quarter. Abel succeeded legendary investor Warren Buffett, 96, at the start of this year. Buffett continues to control roughly 13% of Berkshire common stock, Reuters said Monday, after the former CEO donated $5.5 billion to nonprofit foundations.  Berkshire boosted its stake in Delta as the Atlanta-based carrier's shares tumbled 11% in the third quarter, hurt by  rising jet fuel prices due to the U.S.-Iran war that pressured the entire airline industry. That marked the stock's worst quarterly performance since the first quarter of 2025, when it plunged 28%. Delta last month also cut its full-year earnings forecast, citing a surge in fuel costs. To be sure, buying that dip has been a winning investment thus far. Delta is up 3.8% so far in the fourth quarter, while the S&P 500 has dropped 3.1%. Shares are also up nearly 15% over the past month.Selling some Bank of AmericaBerkshire also trimmed its holding in Bank of America by nearly 6%, selling more than $1.6 billion worth of stock. BofA was under pressure in the third quarter, falling more than 4%, as interest rates surged alongside stubbornly high inflation and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve monetary policy. At one point in September the 30-year Treasury bond yield surged above 5.6% to its highest level since 2002.Despite the share sale, Bank of America remains a top Berkshire Hathaway holding, with the conglomerate's stake valued at $24.8 billion at the end of the third quarter. Berkshire also initiated a position in Bending Spoons and nearly doubled its stake in homebuilder Lennar in the latest quarter.

schema.headline: Berkshire Hathaway raised its stake in Delta in the third quarter. It also trimmed a key bank holding

title: Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness made AI bets again before October rout
description: Leopold AschenbrennerPhoto: Josh EdelsonLeopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapse
body: Leopold AschenbrennerPhoto: Josh EdelsonLeopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapsed in July, loaded back up on AI stocks as it returned to the financial markets at the end of the third quarter. But all of its holdings are down big the last month and a half. According to a new regulatory filing, as the fund got back on its feet Aschenbrenner took an equity position in Australian neocloud company SharonAI valued at more than $440 million, along with equity stakes in AI-centric plays Cleanspark, IREN, Bitdeer Technologies and Fermi. The Cleanspark stake is worth almost $39 million, while Iren and Bitdeer stakes are more than $21 million and more than $20 million, respectively. Fermi, meanwhile, has a value of more than $11 million.The fund also owned call options at the end of September in neocloud Nebius, memory chip name Sandisk, the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) and data center power play Bloom Energy. Sandisk and Nebius were key holdings that almost took out his fund over the summer.All of these Situational Awareness holdings have been routed since Sept. 30. SharonAI is at the top of that list, seeing a 58% loss in October. It's also fallen 11% so far this month. IREN was down 41% in October, while Nebius declined 35%. Last week, Nebius plummeted more than 16% in a single day after the company issued a weak full-year forecast.It's not known whether the hedge fund manager got out of those positions during the October AI selloff. The 13F filing is just a snapshot of what the hedge fund held at the end of the quarter.Aschenbrenner — who launched the fund in 2024 after rising to fame that same year with his AI manifesto also entitled Situational Awareness — re-entered financial markets a bit in September, sources told CNBC at the time.The Monday filing shows he picked up right where he left off. The near-collapse of his hedge fund over the summer forced him to sell all of its public equity positions to Ken Griffin's Citadel. The fund had $45 billion in assets at its peak, but that tumbled to around $10 billion, consisting mostly of private stakes.Stocked tethered to the AI trade took a hit in the most recent quarter as investors grew concerned about a slowdown in development of the technology. Those fears were spurred by comments from industry leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman back in September, with the latter saying that the company going public this year would be "ill-advised."Since then, pressure on the trade has only continued.In recent weeks, investors have worried about how Democratic wins in the midterm elections could hinder data center development, whether some technology companies are using too much debt to finance the AI buildout and what role Nvidia will play in that financing with Jensen Huang now out as CEO at the company.Losses in Nvidia as well as other AI-related stocks dragged down the three leading U.S. indexes during Monday's session as investors continued to assess the fallout of Huang's departure.

schema.headline: Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness made AI bets again before October rout

title: Novo says Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial
description: A Wegovy injection pen arranged in Waterbury, Vermont, US, on Monday, April 28, 2025. Shelby Knowles | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNovo on Monday released
body: A Wegovy injection pen arranged in Waterbury, Vermont, US, on Monday, April 28, 2025. Shelby Knowles | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNovo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial. When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. The detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications."This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," said Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity. In 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040. While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6. In Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.But more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September. "We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina said.Novo said Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The company added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids. Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said. "That is something that is still an evidence gap," she said, pointing to the potential of future research.

schema.headline: Novo says Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial

title: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting
description: Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) speaks during a press conference following the weekly policy luncheon, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., June 3, 2025
body: Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) speaks during a press conference following the weekly policy luncheon, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., June 3, 2025.Annabelle Gordon | ReutersSen. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.Read more CNBC news on NvidiaHow Trump traded Nvidia stock as he championed the chipmakerTrump says Nvidia scandal did not put U.S. national security 'at risk,' defends LutnickNvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on China workaround of restrictionsNvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang's exitThe tech world's calls for Huang to return to Nvidia are growingNvidia stock slides as investors weigh Huang resignationMegaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probeAlice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls."The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act, which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons, who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology.""America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick to testify before his committee in December.Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

schema.headline: Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting

title: China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin historic summit. What will be on the agenda?
description: Russian artist Alexey Sergienko unveils his new pop art painting dubbed "Shenzhen, 26" in Saint Petersburg on November 12, 2026.Olga Maltseva | Afp |
body: Russian artist Alexey Sergienko unveils his new pop art painting dubbed "Shenzhen, 26" in Saint Petersburg on November 12, 2026.Olga Maltseva | Afp | Getty ImagesChina confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders. That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine. While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025. "For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors. Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines. Uncertain agenda The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI. The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda. "He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call. The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said. China has no interest in engaging in nuclear disarmament talks until it achieves parity with the U.S. in about 10 years, said David Roche, strategist at Quantum Strategy. watch nowPutin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today. The summit will likely yield little concrete result, but presents an "almost 100% photo op" that lifts China's status and power at the top table, said Roche, while Trump's political standing slides. Nvidia and the chip-smuggling issues involving a suspected Chinese spy will stay off the agenda, as Trump steers clear of thorny issues where he is unlikely to claim success.China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election.  China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement. "Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability." A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship. Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP. U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

schema.headline: China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin historic summit. What will be on the agenda?

title: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
description: Sankaet Pathak, CEO and founder of Foundation, a company that builds a humanoid robot Phantom-01, poses for a photo during an interview with Reuters a
body: Sankaet Pathak, CEO and founder of Foundation, a company that builds a humanoid robot Phantom-01, poses for a photo during an interview with Reuters at his company's factory in San Francisco, California, U.S., February 4, 2026. Aleksandra Michalska | ReutersFoundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company.The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts. "What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview.'Plain sight'That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business."We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high-five you, they follow your commands."Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism."Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight."Phantom-01, a humanoid robot developed by San Francisco-based startup Foundation for military purposes, sits at the company's factory in San Francisco, California, U.S., February 4, 2026. Aleksandra Michalska | ReutersEric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts."While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal. In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors, claims the automaker rejected.Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.Rescue loan?Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company's financial disclosures, the people said."This is what happens in a company with no governance," said one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?"Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages. The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.Missing moneyBefore Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks. Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.-backed accounts.While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC Chair Jelena McWilliams, said as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula. Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, The Wall Street Journal reported last year. The Journal report didn't mention Pathak specifically.The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview."I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump said. "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job."

title: Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
description: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, speaks during the Federal Reserve's Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference at the Federal Reserv
body: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, speaks during the Federal Reserve's Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco in San Francisco, California, US, on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesArtificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact."We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear. The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.  With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy. Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend. It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island. Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said. Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear. The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his longstanding critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs. Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking. The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event. Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said. "To the extent our economy is a free-market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."Warsh returned repeatedly to one scenario for the economy that draws on past experience. The so-called China shock unfolded after that country joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and moved heavily into low-cost manufacturing. Americans saw prices on clothing and furniture drop rapidly, for instance, but at the cost of severe job losses. One widely cited estimate found the U.S. lost a million manufacturing jobs and 2.4 million jobs overall in the years that followed. Warsh suggested to one of the panelists that the widespread adoption of AI might produce its own version of the China shock, this time focused on service workers. "I don't want to hold this too tightly," Warsh said. "But if in some ways over the last generation or generation and a half, the China shock, for lack of a better word, lowered prices of goods in the United States, the way that I heard you talking about the philosophy of this new technology is it might do something for services."In other words, AI could do, say, legal or administrative work more cheaply than a human. That could lower prices but put many people out of a job.Warsh asked panelists whether "we should expect disinflation over the medium term, from what AI could do to services."They largely suggested it was possible, which could mean the Fed might eventually want to lower interest rates over the long term. But at the end of the day, it is Warsh and his fellow Fed members who will need to have conviction on the answer. There are still many steps between the task force discussion and any kind of change in Fed policy. First, the three task force members will have to assemble their points of view into a report for Warsh sometime in the next few months. Then the Fed itself will need to debate those results and decide whether or how to use them to shape monetary policy. But with AI growing bigger every day, the Fed may need to make up its mind sooner rather than later.

schema.headline: Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means

title: Kalshi plans to launch stock trading soon
description: watch nowLeading prediction market platform Kalshi will offer stock trading within the next few months, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.Th
body: watch nowLeading prediction market platform Kalshi will offer stock trading within the next few months, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.The platform's move to offer equity trading is the boldest so far in its ongoing push into traditional financial markets and comes amid an escalating fight by states and lawmakers against its sports trading business. Sports contracts continue to account for a large share of trading on the platform.In September, the platform introduced perpetual futures tied to precious metals such as gold and silver after it had originally filed in July to offer beyond prediction market event contracts with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal regulator overseeing derivatives contracts. Perpetual futures are futures-style contracts that have no expiration date. Kalshi also received approval to list perpetual futures tied to cryptocurrencies in late May.The prediction market's stock trading offering was enabled by its purchase of broker-dealer FB Securities in July, the source said. FB Securities was founded in Delaware in 2024 and became registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission in December 2025. The broker did not respond to a request for comment.The Wall Street Journal first reported that Kalshi plans to introduce stock trading. Shares of Robinhood, which offers some prediction markets alongside equity trading, fell on Monday, though the stock was already lower amid a broader market sell-off. Robinhood closed down by 7.8%.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Kalshi plans to launch stock trading soon
